title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap, they mostly rely on knowledge reuse or summarization, an approach that is often constrained by directly retrieval without any adaptation for the current task, while the retrieved memory may contain much history noises waiting to be preprocessed. In contrast, MAS characterized by task-specific guidance often lack long-term memory specifically designed for the guidance. To address these challenges, we propose M-Plan, a closed-loop MAS framework that integrates long-term and short-term memory. By combining global-local and past-current guidance, M-Plan enhances agents' performance on multi-turn tasks while maintaining a plug-and-play design. During task execution, agents receive task-specific milestones and insights, and are provided with local hints only when confusion arises, which form global-local guidance together. These guidance generation and utilization construct the short-term memory as well. After task completion, relevant information about the current task is optimized or reorganized before being sent to the long-term memory storage for future retrieval. The designments mentioned above build a comprehensive framework different from other individual long-term or short-term memory works. Extensive experiments on multi-turn tasks including ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models demonstrate that M-Plan outperforms multiple baseline methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

title: Tailoring Dielectric Relaxation and Charge Transport in Amorphous Ge-Te-Se Phase-Change Materials through Yttrium Incorporation
abstract: The Te(1-x)(GeSe0.5)Yx (x = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15) alloys were prepared by a melt-quenching method and characterized using dielectric spectroscopy. The dielectric parameters and electrical conductivity were evaluated to assess their potential for phase-change memory and other electronic applications. The temperature and frequency dependence of the dielectric constants, ac conductivity, and dielectric loss of prepared chalcogenide glassy alloys were investigated over the frequency range 1 Hz - 1 MHz, and the temperature range 302 - 422 K, below the glass transition temperature. Both dielectric loss and dielectric constant were found to decrease with increasing frequency and decreasing temperature. The observed dielectric loss change was interpreted using the Guintini model of dielectric dispersion, correlated barrier hopping (CBH) model, and orientation polarization. The Cole-Cole analysis confirmed a distribution of relaxation times and yielded activation energies consistent with the CBH conduction mechanism. The frequency dependence of the ac conductivity follows the power law (Aωs), where the frequency exponent (s < 1) decreases with increasing temperature, further supporting the CBH conduction mechanism. The incorporation of Y increases the density of localized tail states, resulting in enhanced ac conductivity. These findings suggest that the investigated materials are promising candidates for future phase-change memory and other electronic device applications.

title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents
abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on reusable skills. However, scaling skill libraries makes efficient and accurate skill use difficult. Full skill loading incurs high token and runtime overhead. In contrast, flat semantic retrieval treats skills as independent text entries, ignoring dependencies, execution order, state transitions, and data flow constraints. We propose SPEM, a lightweight structure-aware procedural memory framework for efficient skill use in LLM-based agents. SPEM maintains Atomic Skill Memory for individual skills and Skill-DAG Memory for reusable compositions derived from successful executions. For a new task, SPEM reuses high-confidence Skill-DAG templates when available. Otherwise, it retrieves atomic skills and invokes Skill-GNN for state- and structure-aware skill selection. Successful executions are written back as new Skill-DAGs, allowing procedural memory to accumulate over time. Experiments on ALFWorld and SkillsBench show that SPEM achieves the best overall effectiveness--efficiency trade-off, reaching 87.1% ALFWorld success and 38.38% SkillsBench reward while reducing token and runtime costs against strong baselines.

title: 3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory -bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near- memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic. To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory -Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ over the strongest NMP baselines, with 2.11\% additional logic-die area.

title: Migrate Computation, Not Data: Fault Recovery in Neuromorphic Many-Core Systems
abstract: As neuromorphic systems scale to thousands of near- memory cores, aging-induced permanent faults in neuron-update datapaths become an important obstacle to long-term deployment. Existing online recovery methods typically retire a faulty core and migrate its neurons, along with their weights and membrane states, to healthy cores. This whole-core treatment incurs high recovery traffic and makes recovery depend on scarce destinations; at high utilization, there may be enough surviving compute capacity but insufficient free storage to copy the affected neuron context. This paper presents SpikeRelay, an online recovery framework for diagnosed compute-unit faults. SpikeRelay exploits the fact that, in many neuromorphic cores, the compute datapath, local SRAM, and router are distinct modules: a compute fault need not destroy stored weights and states or disconnect the core from the NoC. Instead of retiring a faulty core and migrating its neuron data, SpikeRelay converts the faulty core into a storage-and-forwarding node while offloading neuron-update computation to a healthy rescue core. This decoupling of storage and computation eliminates recovery-time data migration and greatly reduces spare-SRAM requirements. Consequently, SpikeRelay sustains 100\% recovery at 92.2\% SRAM utilization and a 50\% fault rate, whereas the best baseline achieves only 22.1\%.

title: VS-Flash: Harnessing Vector Search with Computational Memory -Semantic Flash
abstract: As generative AI continues to evolve, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are driving rapid growth in vector database capacity requirements. As datasets outgrow host DRAM, vector databases rely on MMap-based serving over SSDs to extend capacity. However, high-fan-out ANN searches generate concurrent irregular accesses that contend for host memory and storage resources, degrading bulk throughput and inflating tail latency under mixed workloads. In this paper, we address these challenges through memory -semantic capacity and workload-aware compute placement. VS-Flash exposes flash as a large-capacity memory -semantic space and dynamically selects the execution engine according to runtime query and workload characteristics. It offloads throughput-oriented large-batch queries to a Computational Memory -Semantic Flash (CMS-Flash) device, while executing latency-sensitive small-batch queries on the host CPU. Both paths access the same resident segments, avoiding a separate host-DRAM replica. Across three billion-scale datasets, VS-Flash improves bulk-search throughput over vanilla Milvus by 36.8X on average, with up to a 57.4X improvement. Under mixed workloads, VS-Flash reduces the p99 latency of latency-sensitive requests by up to 24.8X while sustaining device-side bulk search. These results show that VS-Flash delivers scalable vector search beyond host DRAM capacity while jointly improving bulk throughput and small-request tail latency.

title: LAMB: Latent Multi-Hypothesis Beliefs for Long-Horizon Large Language Agents
abstract: Long-horizon language agents require compact memories that retain interaction evidence while preserving competing hypotheses about unobserved states. Although effective, many belief-state methods encode memory in discrete natural language, where repeated compression can omit evidence or prematurely discard plausible alternatives. We introduce LAMB, a recurrent framework for latent multi-hypothesis beliefs. A Common--Delta factorization combines a shared Common state for interaction evidence with weighted Delta components for competing hypotheses. Relative evidence from action-outcome predictions guides recurrent hypothesis updates without generating textual memory. A context-conditioned readout exposes hypotheses separately to the policy through a fixed-token belief prefix in the default configuration. The belief modules and policy are jointly trained using action imitation and auxiliary state, outcome, and observation-discrimination objectives. Across ALFWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, LAMB matches or outperforms PABU, improving ALFWorld SR@30 and ScienceWorld success by 6.0 and 22.0 percentage points, respectively, and Crafter achievement progress by 26.37 points. On ALFWorld, it also reduces the redundant-action rate by 17.70 percentage points. These results support latent multi-hypothesis beliefs as compact memory for effective long-horizon decision making

title: Emulating DGEMM and ZGEMM with INT8 Matrix Engines on Intel Arc GPUs: Ozaki Scheme II on the Xe2 Architecture
abstract: Double-precision matrix multiplication, real (DGEMM) and complex (ZGEMM), dominates the run time of dense linear algebra and electronic-structure codes. On affordable GPUs, however, FP64 throughput is a small and shrinking fraction of the throughput of the low-precision matrix engines. Ozaki scheme II closes this gap by reducing a floating-point matrix product to a handful of exact INT8 products followed by a Chinese-remainder reconstruction; the number of products sets the accuracy. We present what is, to our knowledge, the first implementation of Ozaki scheme II for Intel GPUs. Written in SYCL on top of oneMKL, it runs entirely on the device and exposes the full BLAS dgemm/zgemm interface. Making the scheme fast on the Xe2 (Battlemage) architecture required keeping FP64 arithmetic out of all memory -bound kernels, a branch-free residue computation, an FP32 evaluation of the CRT quotient with a proven safety margin, 16-bit limb arithmetic in the reconstruction, and work-arounds for performance cliffs of the vendor INT8 GEMM. On an Intel Arc Pro B60 (24 GB) the emulated DGEMM reaches 17.3, 12.1 and 9.3 TFLOP/s with $s=8$, 12 and 16 moduli at $N=8192$, and up to 21.1 TFLOP/s overall, i.e. 12-28x the native FP64 DGEMM of the same board. The emulated ZGEMM, which uses the 3M form exactly in integer arithmetic, reaches up to 27.4 TFLOP/s and is 13.7-17.8x faster than native ZGEMM for $N\ge4096$ at $s=16$. With $s\ge16$ the results are correctly rounded for well-scaled inputs and, using an extended-width residue path ($s=20$-24), also for inputs with wide exponent ranges, whereas native DGEMM rounds only 2-13% of the entries correctly. We also report worst-case accuracy, phase breakdowns, energy, an ablation study, a comparison with Ozaki scheme I, and a validated performance model.

title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.

title: SARP: An On-SSD Index for KVCache with Fast Prefix Matching and Recovery
abstract: Distributed LLM serving relies on a global index to locate reusable key-value cache (KVCache) blocks through prefix matching. Losing the index after a crash or restart forces affected requests to recompute existing KVCache on GPUs. Persisting the index restores access after a failure. Existing persistent indexes face a tension between prefix-matching performance and recovery time. A snapshot-backed in- memory index supports fast prefix matching, but rebuilding the full index delays recovery. An on-SSD index avoids this rebuild, but adds storage accesses to prefix matching. Our core insight is that extending a matched prefix over a short span typically requires distinguishing only a few token sequences, suggesting that sparse in- memory routing state may suffice. Prefix matching also accesses block metadata in sequence order, allowing metadata for consecutive blocks to be retrieved together. We present SARP (Sparse Adaptive Routing and Packing), an on-SSD KVCache index for fast recovery and prefix matching. SARP groups consecutive block IDs and metadata into segments to amortize storage accesses across multiple blocks. A compact in- memory routing directory identifies candidate segments using entries at selected block positions. SARP limits segment retrievals and uses compact filters to prioritize candidates with longer potential matches. After retrieval, SARP verifies block IDs against the query and reuses only KVCache blocks covered by the verified prefix. After a restart, SARP restores the sparse routing directory from a snapshot. Across four multi-turn chat and agentic workloads, SARP recovers 8.0x to 77.5x faster than the in- memory index baselines and delivers 1.15x to 66.6x the request throughput of the on-SSD index baselines, while reusing only 0.0030% to 0.029% fewer tokens than exact prefix matching.

title: SpecKCast: Spectral Kalman Forecasting for Diffusion Acceleration
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity image and video generation, but they suffer from substantial inference costs due to repeated transformer evaluations across many denoising steps. Feature caching reduces this cost by reusing features across denoising steps. Recent forecasting methods extend this idea by extrapolating features to skipped steps instead of reusing them. However, existing forecasting methods extrapolate the features they predict uniformly, even though the spatial-frequency components of these features change most at different stages of denoising. They also overlook that denoising progresses nonuniformly, so equal step intervals can correspond to very different amounts of change. These mismatches amplify forecast errors as more steps are skipped, limiting the achievable acceleration. We propose SpecKCast, a training-free method that forecasts the model output in the frequency domain. SpecKCast applies a 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT) to the output and tracks each coefficient with a lightweight Kalman filter along a band-specific time coordinate derived from the noise schedule. The filter tracks each coefficient's value and rate of change, and the transformer is evaluated only when the filter's forecast uncertainty exceeds a threshold. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1-14B, and HunyuanVideo show that SpecKCast achieves a better trade-off between acceleration and fidelity than existing caching and forecasting methods, reaching up to 6x speedup with less than 0.05 GiB of additional memory .

title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.

title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

title: Mechanical angular momentum loss at $\mathcal{O}(G^4)$ from static and radiative gravitons
abstract: We determine the loss of mechanical angular momentum $L^μ_{\rm loss}$ of two gravitationally scattering bodies at $\mathcal{O}(G^4)$ using worldline quantum field theory (WQFT). The gravitational memory effect, a phenomenon of the early- and late-time behaviour of the gravitational field, leads to static contributions to $L^μ_{\rm loss}$. We illuminate how these arise: the linear memory contributes through so-called static correlators, while the nonlinear memory vanishes at this order due to symmetry considerations. The computation of the remaining, dynamical part resembles that of the $\mathcal{O}(G^4)$ impulse. We generate its integrand using a reformulation of the WQFT Feynman rules that conserves four-momentum at every vertex and plainly exhibits the classical loops. The three-loop integrals are reduced to master integrals, whose differential equations and boundary matching in the post-Newtonian limit we describe in some detail. In contrast to conservative effects at this order, only polylogarithms appear. While individual contributions to the dynamical part are divergent, these cancel in $L^μ_{\rm loss}$. The quadratic-in-radiation part of our result reproduces earlier results, while the complete result agrees with existing post-Newtonian results.

title: High-Accuracy Propagation-Assisted Local Decoding for Fast Transversal Clifford Circuits
abstract: We benchmark the Iterative Redecode Scheme (IRS) on fast transversal Clifford circuits, achieving high-accuracy correlated decoding using local memory -style detectors and decoders. On a deep random Clifford benchmark, IRS yields approximately $4\times$ lower logical failure rates than the ghost protocol at $d=11$ with matched buffers, and $15\times$ lower rates than logical observable matching (LOM). In three-block GHZ preparation, IRS achieves $2\times$ lower logical error rates than reliable logical Pauli-product decoding with matched initialisation, improving to $25\times$ at $d=19$ with $\lceil d/2\rceil$ full initialisation rounds. We place IRS, which builds on Wan et al.'s scheme, within a broader propagation-assisted local (PAL) framework, where local decoders exchange messages rather than decoding a global hypergraph. IRS alternates local minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) on memory -equivalent detector error models (DEMs) with Pauli-frame propagation and detector updates across transversal CNOT layers, seeking local error estimates consistent with the global detector record. Prior-informed DEMs account for probabilities of propagated errors missing from the memory -equivalent model, improving initial decoding and reducing logical error rates. Zero-weight physical Pauli mechanisms enable inference and propagation of initially indeterminate stabilizer outcomes. Error rates saturate after a few iterations even for deep, adversarial alternating-tCNOT circuits, allowing iteration caps with negligible loss of accuracy. We find syndrome-extraction buffers of order $\lfloor d/4\rfloor$ sufficient for distance-dependent error suppression in the demanding regimes studied. The approach extends to other local decoders and CSS codes; for repeated logical $S$ gates, IRS achieves approximately $4$ to $10\times$ lower logical error rates than LOM, depending on initialisation.

title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
abstract: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.

title: Injection of Space Radiation Errors on Low-power NVM using Generative Deep Learning
abstract: We develop an error model for a Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) device that represents the effects of physical faults experienced in a CubeSat mission in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The CubeSat carries an off-the-shelf low-power Ferroelectric RAM (FRAM) chip and runs repeated read/write tests according to a predefined pattern. We compare every memory snapshot received from the satellite with a reference bitmap to identify bit errors. We visually analyze erroneous values distributions in the memory snapshots and we understand that they are frequently distributed according to regular spatial patterns. We define a generative deep learning technique to automatically learn these spatial patterns and to synthetically generate additional error patterns mimicking the observed ones. The model is capable at producing memory errors for general application-level experimentation. Our preliminary validation indicates that when comparing the model output with the data we collect, 0.92 of the generated bit flips correspond to bit flips in the memory snapshots and the model captures 0.91 of the observed bit flips. A comparison of the spatial distribution of bit flips in 10,000 generated error patterns also provides a Wasserstein distance of 0.073, indicating that the two distributions differ by roughly 7% of the maximum possible displacement of their probability masses.

title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers
abstract: A liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) exhibits a two-way coupling between its mesogen order and network elasticity: the mesogen order sets the undeformed network conformation, and the network deformation reorients the mesogens. This coupling gives rise to large, reversible stimuli-responsive actuation, as well as to soft elasticity, a finite deformation at nearly zero stress. This article reviews the elastic theory of ideal LCEs, bridging single-chain statistics and continuum constitutive models. The "ideal" elastic behavior rests on the assumption of anisotropic Gaussian chains that retain no memory of the crosslinking state, such that rotating the director costs no free energy. The corresponding neo-classical free energy of a monodomain LCE is non-quasi-convex, with a continuous family of stress-free ground states, leading to thermally induced spontaneous deformation and soft elasticity accommodated by coexisting stripe domains. The quasi-convex relaxation of the free energy classifies the behavior of polydomain LCEs into three phases, each with a distinct macroscopic mechanical response depending on the stretch state. The ideal elastic theory can be further extended to incorporate additional behaviors and physical processes, including thermo- and photomechanical coupling, Frank elasticity from director distortion, semi-soft or non-soft behavior arising from network nonideality, and temperature- and rate-dependent viscoelasticity.

title: Tandem: Serving Hybrid Linear-Attention GUI Agents on Mobile NPUs
abstract: Smartphone GUI agents complete tasks in mobile apps by repeatedly reading the screen and asking a model for the next action. Mobile neural processing units (NPUs) enable local execution, keeping screen contents on the phone, but model latency accumulates with every action. Hybrid linear attention models reduce memory requirements, yet reusing their recurrent state requires checkpoints at the appropriate input positions. Agent requests retain instructions but rewrite recent history, so checkpoint policies designed for chat continuation can miss reusable prefixes. Retaining rollback states for speculative decoding can also move prompt processing off the NPU's matrix unit, adding overhead that outweighs decoding savings on short action outputs. A loaded model can further hold the NPU awake between tasks. We present Tandem, a runtime for hybrid GUI agents on mobile NPUs. Tandem saves recurrent state where consecutive prompts diverge, allowing later requests to reuse previously processed context. It keeps most prefill on the matrix unit and produces rollback states through a short per-token tail. Its verification kernel reads each weight block once for all proposed tokens. Between request bursts, Tandem releases NPU power votes without unloading the model. We implement Tandem in llama.cpp and evaluate it on recorded agent interactions across two Snapdragon generations. On a Snapdragon 8 Elite, Tandem reduces per-step latency by 30% for text-based screen descriptions and 16% for screenshots relative to llama.cpp's fastest NPU configuration, reduces energy per text step by 33%, and lowers standby power with the model loaded from 0.76 to 0.22 W.

title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents
abstract: Long-horizon embodied agents face temporal confusion and incomplete or distorted records, recurring errors from fixed memory rules, and growing storage and retrieval costs. We present BetaMem, a framework for building and evolving traceable long-term memory through six linked layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural memory. A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Atomic tools frame storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost-utility allocation under storage and read budgets. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. Training the model for memory generation raises the contract pass rate from 50.9% to 86.2% while reducing output tokens per stored action by 47.3%. A separate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluation on EMem-Bench achieves an average success rate of 38.4% and an average error recurrence rate of 24.9%. We perform best among evaluated methods using comparably sized open-source models. Category results show that we have advantages in integrating information across observations, recalling events over long histories, and inferring personal habits.

title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.

title: UnO-NeSy: Optimizing Neuro-Symbolic Computing with Unified FeFET Based In- Memory System
abstract: Neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence (NeSy AI) combines neural perception with symbolic reasoning, enabling logical reasoning. Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is promising for NeSy AI, owing to its high parallelism and strong robustness to noise. However, the dense neural operations and memory -intensive symbolic inference in NeSy impose a severe " memory wall" bottleneck. Existing NeSy accelerators either focus solely on symbolic kernels or rely on conventional digital architectures, lacking a unified and energy-efficient hardware substrate. Moreover, exploring optimal hardware design configurations often requires costly trial-and-error. In this work, we propose UnO-NeSy, a unified CiM framework for optimizing NeSy computing. UnO-NeSy consists of UnO-CiM, an ultra-low-power NeSy architecture based on a homogeneous 2FeFET--2R compute-in- memory (CiM) array that supports both neural computation and HDC reasoning, and UnO-Sim, a cross-workload, end-to-end CiM simulator that models device non-idealities, neural quantization effects, and HDC execution behavior for accurate system-level evaluation. Built on UnO-Sim, we further develop an automated optimizer to identify workload-specific operating points under coupled energy, accuracy, and hardware constraints. By optimizing the operating configuration of the baseline 2FeFET--2R design, UnO-NeSy achieves $61.8\%$ higher energy efficiency and $38.2\%$ lower full-system inference energy. Across seven RAVEN configurations, UnO-NeSy achieves $96.2\%$ average reasoning accuracy under hardware non-idealities, demonstrating a practical and scalable path toward ultra-low-power NeSy hardware.

title: U(1) Current Diffusion in Gauss-Bonnet Holography
abstract: We study holographic $U(1)$ charge transport using a probe Maxwell field in a five-dimensional Gauss-Bonnet-AdS black-brane background. Within the all-order linearised fluid/gravity framework, we derive the off-shell constitutive relation and determine the diffusion function and electric and magnetic conductivities analytically in the hydrodynamic regime and numerically at generic frequency and momentum. To first order in the Gauss-Bonnet coupling, the leading diffusion constant remains unchanged in our normalization, while its frequency dependence and the electric conductivity receive nontrivial corrections. The deformation also generates a nonvanishing leading magnetic conductivity. Beyond the hydrodynamic regime, it modifies the transport profiles while preserving the damped behaviour of the diffusion function. The corresponding memory kernel vanishes at negative times, supporting a retarded constitutive response.

title: ScopeMem: Latent Memory That Learns Where to Revise Frozen GUI Agents
abstract: Latent memory is gaining ground as a lightweight history supplement for GUI agents. It supplies history to a frozen vision-language model via prefix vectors trained with step-wise cross-entropy (CE). While resulting gains are naturally attributed to encoded history, our controlled experiments show they primarily stem from action revision. The prefix learns to alter the model's default actions. However, this revision is unscoped because step-wise CE pushes outputs toward reference actions at every step without explicitly preserving correct decisions. Consequently, it repairs errors but also breaks 8-13% of initially correct answers. Overall accuracy metrics hide these losses. We therefore propose ScopeMem, a latent-memory method for scoped revision. Its encoder conditions prefix generation on the model's initial answer and is trained to correct errors while preserving correct decisions. On the controlled ablation set, ScopeMem reduces the share of broken correct decisions to 5.6% while repairing more errors than any evaluated CE-trained prefix. On AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, and zero-shot AITW, ScopeMem outperforms all evaluated prompting and latent-memory baselines, enabling a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B to match or surpass GUI-specialized agents and Qwen3-VL-32B.

title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging
abstract: Generative deep learning methods such as Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks or Diffusion Models have achieved remarkable results in image synthesis. In particular, Diffusion Models have demonstrated superior image fidelity and sample diversity compared to other approaches on standard benchmarks, while also offering more flexible training dynamics as evidenced both in natural image domains and in medical applications. In medical imaging including Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Positron Emission Tomography, such models have various important use-cases including data augmentation, domain transfer, image reconstruction, inpainting, image augmentation and artifact correction. Further, generated images can be conditioned on patient characteristics, medical reports, segmentation masks or other images. Specific challenges arise due to the 3D volumetric nature of medical images, which translate to substantial demands in terms of memory , compute, and training data. This article provides a comparative overview of 3D Diffusion Models which have been developed for medical images, with a focus on current performance, limitations, and an outlook for future work.

title: YUTELA: A Scalable Edge Cloud AIoT System for Multi-Site Video Anomaly Detection with Scene Specific Adaptation
abstract: Building upon our previous Ancilia framework, this work presents \emph{YUTELA}, an edge--server--cloud AIoT system for long-term, multi-site video anomaly detection. YUTELA replaces workstation-based on-site processing with NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge devices and redesigns the multi-camera pipeline through camera batching and redistribution, shared memory , reduced inter-stage data transfer, task integration, and TensorRT-accelerated inference. It maintains a separate anomaly model per camera, retrained on a centralized GPU server once enough recent pseudo-normal data are collected, with updated weights returned to the edge. With eight cameras, TensorRT increases throughput from 14.17 to 29.94 FPS under normal density, and the optimized edge node exceeds the throughput of the workstation-based Ancilia system in seven of nine workload settings, reaching up to 2.03 times its throughput at extreme density. This gain comes at the cost of higher latency under lighter loads with four or eight streams. YUTELA was then operated continuously for 170 hours at four public sites using 31 existing CCTV cameras. The deployment shows that runtime load is driven by scene activity and input frame rate rather than by camera count, and that retraining frequency varies by about three times across sites. The 101 automatically triggered training events occupied only about 6.6\% of a single GPU, indicating that one global node can support adaptation for tens of sites. Mean end-to-end alert latency ranged from 6.8 to 15.4~s depending on site traffic and anomaly type. These results show that YUTELA enables practical multi-camera edge processing with low-cost, camera-specific adaptation across heterogeneous sites.

title: Progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory for incomplete multimodal brain tumor segmentation
abstract: Brain tumor segmentation uses complementary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences, but some sequences may be unavailable in practice. Their absence changes the information available for segmenting different tumor regions. Fusion methods can support different input subsets. However, fusion at several scales does not by itself specify how tumor evidence is retained and updated to guide fusion at later stages. We propose a progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory network (PMTM) for segmentation from any non-empty subset of T1ce, T1, FLAIR, and T2. PMTM maintains a compact state for the current subject across the encoder stages. At each stage, we use assignment maps to pool spatial features into ordered evidence vectors for each available modality. We average these vectors across the available modalities, and a learned gate combines this evidence with the previous state. The up- dated state guides residual fusion at that stage and is used in the state update at the next stage. A modality-token mixer also models interactions among the available modalities at each stage. We apply semantic supervision to the assignment maps at all four stages. We evaluate PMTM on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI across all 15 non-empty modality subsets. Averaged over the three tumor regions and the 15 subsets, PMTM achieves Dice scores of 75.31%, 77.54%, and 80.47% on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI, respectively. These scores are higher than those of RobustSeg, RFNet, and mmFormer in our experiments on each dataset. Component ablations and internal state analysis are performed on BraTS2020.

title: Learning What to Remember: Resource-Efficient Self-Improvement for Lifelong Agents
abstract: Self-improving agents aim to continuously improve their behavior by learning from experience after deployment. However, accumulating and reusing more experience does not necessarily lead to better decisions, particularly when generation, interaction, and memory resources are jointly constrained. Under such stringent constraints, we find that several existing lifelong-memory methods provide limited benefits over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a fundamental challenge for resource-efficient self-improvement: agents must learn not only which past experiences are relevant, but which are actually worth reusing to improve future decisions. When memory capacity and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving an ineffective experience can consume scarce resources and hinder downstream execution. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight feedback-driven memory adaptation framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback. Without updating the backbone model, TokenWorth uses the learned worth to guide both experience retrieval and bounded memory management, enabling the agent to continually adapt how it reuses accumulated experience. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods under the specified resource budgets. These results suggest that effective self-improvement under resource constraints depends not on accumulating more experience, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth.

title: The Geometry of Agent Memory: Forecasting Retrieval-Bound Memory Failures, and Characterizing Its Limits
abstract: We study whether geometric relationships between conversation turns, memory texts, and queries can predict answer correctness before generation. We evaluate four memory implementations with dense or hybrid retrieval and one observation-summary comparator. We embed these texts in a shared space. A logistic classifier uses 25 features describing query proximity, memory-conversation correspondence, and conversation structure. On LongMemEval-small, pooled AUROC is 0.640 over 2,367 question-system pairs, below a question-difficulty baseline of 0.655. Performance varies by question type: geometry reaches 0.841 on single-session-assistant questions, but system identity alone reaches 0.826. After controlling for difficulty and identity, geometry adds no statistically established pooled improvement (delta = +0.002, 95% CI [-0.010, 0.014]). A fixed-store context-selection experiment finds higher accuracy with proximity-ranked memories than with random subsets, consistent with ordinary retrieval relevance. On LoCoMo, nearest-turn similarity has modest predictive value for single-hop questions and near-chance estimates for several other categories. Training uses correctness labels; prediction uses pre-answer features and no additional LLM generation call. The results characterize associations between memory representations and correctness, rather than establish a reliable deployment diagnostic. In particular, embedding proximity does not verify fact coverage or distinguish memory-construction, retrieval, and generation errors.

title: Parameter-efficient neural computing with programmable photonic meshes
abstract: Memory capacity and bandwidth are becoming major constraints in neural-network computing, motivating parameter-efficient representations that reduce model storage and data movement. Tensor-network methods already enable substantial compression of neural networks, but their structured operations are often poorly matched to conventional processors optimized for dense linear algebra. Such representations can be implemented in photonic hardware, although this typically requires optical architectures tailored to a particular factorization. Here we propose a different approach based on programmable photonic meshes. Compact electronic parameters determine the interferometer phases, while optical interference produces a dense, generally high-rank transformation. Since the parameterization remains electronic, its dimensionality and structure can be changed without modifying the optical circuit. Numerical experiments in end-to-end training demonstrate that the proposed photonic layers match or outperform strongly compressed tensor-train and brickwork layers, often with fewer trainable parameters. Experiments in parameter-efficient fine-tuning of a language model also show advantages over established digital adapters. The reduced trainable state lowers persistent memory requirements and offers the potential to reduce data movement and bandwidth demands.

title: HarnessRL: Co-Evolving Policies with a Just-in-Time Training Harness for Open-Ended RL
abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) trains policies for open-ended generation with natural-language criteria as rewards, but these rewards can become ineffective as training progresses. We identify two failure modes. Under non-discriminative rewards, scores collapse to uniformly low or high values due to insufficient exploration or a mismatch between task difficulty and policy capability. Under spurious rewards, higher scores do not correspond to better responses. Both reflect a training configuration whose task sampling, exploration, and evaluation stay fixed as the policy evolves. We introduce HarnessRL, a training-time harness that co-evolves with the policy through three interfaces for task sampling, rollout guidance, and rubric criteria. HarnessRL maintains a training-time memory from which a harness evolver retrieves within-task history and cross-task evidence. Using this evidence, the evolver attributes each reward failure to the interface whose update can address it. It then runs a proposer and just-in-time critic loop in which the critic accepts a candidate update only after measuring its effect on the current frozen policy, returning rejected candidates for revision. We also curate Rubric-Mix-10k, a five-domain training and evaluation suite for open-ended RL across medical, science, writing, role-play, and instruction-following tasks. On Rubric-Mix-10k, HarnessRL outperforms the strongest baselines by 2.8 to 3.1 points across both 4B and 9B model scales and nearly halves the training steps to its best checkpoint. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Tongyi-ConvAI/Qwen-Character/tree/main/HarnessRL.

title: Signal Design Impacts on GNSS and LEO-PNT L1 Band Acquisition Complexity: A Case Study with Xona Pulsar
abstract: GNSS signal acquisition is the process of detecting and estimating signal parameters by exploiting correlation operations that provide processing gain and enable the detection of signals below the noise floor. The design of an acquisition engine requires balancing achievable sensitivity, computational complexity, memory requirements, power consumption, and implementation complexity. In particular, increasing coherent and non-coherent integration times improves sensitivity but can significantly increase receiver processing requirements, limiting its applicability in low-power and resource-constrained receivers. This paper presents a comparative analysis of L1-band signal acquisition complexity by evaluating the required integration time and corresponding implementation requirements for different signal designs under equivalent acquisition performance targets. The analysis considers the impact of signal characteristics, including spreading codes, secondary codes, modulation, and signal bandwidth, on coherent and non-coherent acquisition performance. For a given attenuation level and target probability of false alarm and detection, the required integration times are derived and translated into acquisition complexity metrics, including arithmetic operations, processing time, and memory requirements. The analysis is applied to Pulsar X1, a LEO-enabled PNT signal, and representative GNSS L1 signals to determine under which attenuation, assistance, and integration conditions the higher received power of LEO-PNT translates into reduced receiver acquisition workload. By relating the required integration to arithmetic operations, processing time, and memory requirements, the study provides a receiver-level comparison relevant to both conventional and snapshot-based receivers, where reducing acquisition processing can directly contribute to lower energy consumption.

title: Pangolin: Efficient DAG-based BFT State-Machine Replication with TEE-Accelerated Commitment
abstract: Currently many Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) protocols use directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to let replicas propose blocks of requests in parallel for improved throughput. Yet, the existing DAG-based designs mainly consider the atomic-broadcast layer: They typically do not describe an efficient client interaction layer, their garbage collection is either unspecified or relies on trusted external storage, and the lowest-latency designs rely on timing assumptions that may be violated in geo-distributed deployments. In this paper, we propose the Pangolin protocol: It introduces a novel low-latency DAG-based atomic broadcast layer and completes it into an efficient state-machine replication (SMR) framework. To preserve system throughput, clients issue requests to a single replica and verify replies efficiently via compact execution proofs. Furthermore, Pangolin introduces a new garbage-collection scheme for DAGs which bounds memory usage even under full asynchrony. Pangolin leverages trusted execution environments to tolerate f Byzantine faults with only n >= 2f + 1 replicas and accelerates vertex commitments significantly: Broadcasting certified vertices requires only a single communication step, and commit rules are refined to commit both frequently and early without revealing the coin-elected anchor. This way, Pangolin overtakes the fastest partially synchronous DAG protocols while being live under asynchrony: In our evaluation, Pangolin achieves an average 1.27x (up to 1.52x) latency speedup over Mysticeti.

title: Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
abstract: Autoregressive Diffusion Transformers have emerged as a powerful paradigm for long video generation. However, they are often constrained by prohibitive computational overhead and substantial memory footprints. This inefficiency arises from dense computation mechanisms that allocate uniform processing resources across all spatiotemporal regions, failing to leverage the inherent temporal redundancy of video where motion is typically confined to sparse areas. In this paper, we propose Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention (DASA), a unified framework that shifts from dense computation to sparse, motion-driven generation to eliminate both storage and computational redundancies. Inspired by video codec principles, our approach explicitly decouples video content into dynamic and static regions. To mitigate memory bottlenecks, we selectively compress the historical KV cache by retaining only dynamic features within the generated chunk. Furthermore, to reduce computational overhead, we employ a region-level computation allocation strategy based on localized dynamics. Additionally, a dynamics-guided distillation method is introduced to enhance performance via a lightweight distillation training process. Experiments on VBench demonstrate that our approach accelerates autoregressive video generation by 2.16x, while preserving high visual fidelity.

title: XGLASS: X-Ray, Gaze and Language Assisted Slice Sequencing for CT Volumes
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve remarkable performance on 2D medical images, such as X-rays or pathology images, while 3D VLMs that directly process CT/MRI volumes lag behind due to limited 3D training data and the predominance of 2D foundation architectures. To leverage powerful 2D VLMs for analyzing medical volumes, which contain hundreds of slices, it is therefore necessary to focus only on those few slices, which are diagnostically relevant. To enable such a prioritization, we propose XGLASS, a method that transfers medical expertise from 2D X-rays to 3D CT for task-aware slice prioritization. XGLASS uses disease-conditioned importance maps derived from language-aligned radiologist gaze on X-rays and spatially aligns them with coronal CT projections, bringing gaze priors and CT content into a shared 2D representation. The fused gaze-prior/CT projection is then used to predict a disease-specific ordering of axial slices, prioritizing diagnostically relevant slices. XGLASS significantly improves budgeted retrieval over 2D and 3D-native baselines, achieving a top-10 hit rate up to 75.9% for the best-performing disease. In practice, this means that after inspecting only the top 10 slices (4.17% of a 240-slice scan), XGLASS identifies a diagnostically relevant slice in more than 75% of cases. For downstream slice-wise finding classification, an XGLASS-selected 30-slice candidate set reduces model calls by 87.5% while improving F1 by 11.3 percentage points over all-slice inference, 4.2 points over the strongest 2D selector, and remains competitive with 3D-native selectors while requiring up to 130.8 times less time and 10.9 times less GPU memory per finding, supporting its use as a lightweight preselector for volumetric CT analysis. The code and pretrained checkpoint are available on https://github.com/michaelgloeckler/XGLASS.

title: Bridging In-Situ Visualization to Game Engines: From ParaView Catalyst via ANARI to Unreal Engine
abstract: In-situ high-performance computing (HPC) simulations produce massive datasets that remain difficult to stream into game engines for interactive visualization. We present an in-situ, disk-free pipeline that couples simulation data to Unreal Engine 5 through ParaView's ANARI rendering API. A modified ANARI-USD device captures Universal Scene Description (USD) scene graphs in memory at the ANARI layer and streams the engine-agnostic USD format through an embedded ZeroMQ broker to visualization clients, where JuSync, middleware with a companion Unreal Engine 5 plugin, parses the geometry as it arrives and routes it to engine rendering components at runtime, producing scenes that are camera-navigable once received. The decoupled design keeps simulation execution independent of visualization load, and clients may connect or disconnect at any time. The pipeline is demonstrated on the JURECA-DC supercomputer at Forschungszentrum Jülich, streaming Free Electron Laser (FEL) simulation data with point clouds of tens of millions of particles.

title: The Fundamental Memory Ceiling of Noisy Quantum Reservoirs
abstract: Fresh qubits, not size, set how long a noisy quantum system can remember. With $k$ input qubits reinitialized per time step, the longest memory any reservoir can attain under depolarizing noise is $\exp[Θ(k)]$ time steps, whatever its size, dynamics, and input encoding. A universal upper bound and an explicit reservoir that attains the exponential scaling establish this optimal resource law. The bound depends on the dynamics only through the entropy that fresh qubits remove per time step, so it holds for any Markovian noisy dynamics without feedback, including measurement-free error correction.

title: Rethinking BPE: Merge Selection as Model Selection
abstract: Subword tokenization methods such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) are a core component of modern language models; yet, tokenizer capacity remains typically determined by a fixed merge budget, chosen heuristically. Since larger vocabularies increase memory usage and computational cost, selecting compact and effective token inventories is essential for efficient language modeling. We study the optimization of a BPE merge budget as a statistical model selection problem and investigate information-theoretic criteria for \emph{computing optimal merge sets} directly from corpus statistics. To further improve the merge selection in limited data conditions, we augment the BPE training corpora with synthetic texts generated from the original data, providing estimates for the unigram and bigram distributions. Experiments across multiple corpora and downstream tasks show that using a principled vocabulary selection technique reduces model size, with little degradation in performance. We further observe that synthetic data can yield better tokenizers, especially in low-resource settings.

title: GeoTrain: Energy-Aware Automatic Parallelism for Foundation Model Training on Heterogeneous Geo-Distributed Resources
abstract: Training foundation models at the frontier typically requires large-scale dedicated and centralized clusters with fast interconnects - infrastructure that is prohibitively expensive and generally accessible only to well-resourced organizations. Decentralized training over pooled, geographically distributed GPUs offers an alternative, but introduces substantial heterogeneity in compute, memory , power, and network performance. Existing distributed training systems are primarily designed for clusters with fast, low-latency interconnects and typically use all available GPUs when configuring parallel training. In geo-distributed environments, however, slower devices and weak network links can become bottlenecks, while optimizing solely for throughput overlooks significant energy cost. We present GeoTrain, an automatic parallelism system that jointly optimizes training performance and energy consumption for heterogeneous geo-distributed GPU environments. GeoTrain simultaneously selects GPUs, partitions model layers, and determines pipeline configurations while accounting for heterogeneous compute, memory , power, and network constraints. To efficiently explore this large combinatorial search space, GeoTrain employs an optimized memetic algorithm with specialized genetic operators and local search. Experiments with decoder-only Transformer models on real-world and simulated heterogeneous topologies demonstrate that GeoTrain reduces iteration time and energy consumption by up to $61.4\%$ and $11.7\%$, respectively, over the existing state-of-the-art approaches. It also finds the exact optimum on verifiable instances and scales beyond exact methods as the number of GPUs increases, while exposing favorable energy-time trade-offs, including cases where its time-optimal distributed training plan is both faster and more energy-efficient than the baselines.

title: VISAGENT: An Agent-Based End-to-End Voice Interaction System
abstract: Voice-based public services have evolved from manual switchboards to intelligent platforms to meet modern user needs. However, current systems remain constrained by rigid menu-driven interaction, fragmented vertical services, and limited extensibility. To address these issues, we present VISAGENT, an agent-based end-to-end voice interaction system for large-scale public services that integrates end-to-end speech interaction, hierarchical agent routing, a scalable voice-agent marketplace, and user memory support. The system replaces menu-driven workflows with natural speech and dynamically dispatches user requests to either a general conversational model or specialized domain agents via a two-level routing paradigm that achieves sub-second intent-to-agent selection over hundreds of agents. User memory informs preference-aware agent selection and supplies relevant preferences and context to selected agents, supporting personalized task execution and reducing the need for users to repeat previously provided information. A voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational entities, enabling dynamic onboarding and ecosystem-level extensibility. We validate VISAGENT through a real-world deployment in China's 114 hotline across multiple service domains. Experimental results demonstrate low-latency full-duplex interaction, robust routing scalability, and competitive speech naturalness. More broadly, this work advocates a shift from isolated voice assistants toward agent-centric conversational infrastructures, providing a general blueprint for building extensible voice-agent systems in public services and beyond.

title: Holistic Buoyancy-Driven Cloud Native Resource Management
abstract: Efficient resource management is a challenge in multi-tenant cloud environments as workloads compete for shared resources such as last-level cache and memory bandwidth, whose congestion can change dynamically as workload composition and resource demands evolve. Existing resource management approaches often rely on static resource requirements or prior workload profiling, limiting their ability to respond to changing resource contention as required in the cloud. In this paper, we leverage workload buoyancy, a runtime framework for capturing workload sensitivity to individual resources and application-level performance, to enable adaptive scheduling and resource management. We propose a holistic approach that incorporates buoyancy into workload scheduling, node-local resource allocation, and workload rescheduling throughout the workload lifecycle. We implement our approach as a Kubernetes-native prototype and evaluate it on a multi-node cluster using diverse cloud workloads under varying levels of resource contention. In a high-congestion scenario, our approach increases the percentage of workloads satisfying their SLOs from 7.74% to 87.8% on average compared with the Kubernetes baseline, while reducing resource congestion, the severity of SLO violations, and cluster fragmentation using limited rescheduling.

title: A Hybrid GPU and Processing-Near- Memory Architecture with Shared DRAM for Efficient Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
abstract: The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) has significantly increased the compute and memory demands of inference serving. A key challenge arises from the mismatch between compute-bound prefill and memory -bound decoding: when executed together, the two phases interfere, while separating them via prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation leads to substantial resource underutilization. Specifically, prefill leaves memory bandwidth underutilized, whereas decoding underutilizes compute resources. Prior approaches, such as GPU Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) partitioning, attempt to improve utilization by spatially dividing GPU resources. However, these approaches remain fundamentally limited, as memory -bound decoding still requires a large number of SMs to saturate bandwidth, reducing the compute resources available for prefill and resulting in an inherent trade-off. To address this limitation, we propose DuoPD, a hybrid PD-disaggregation architecture that integrates lightweight Processing-Near- Memory (PNM) units into the HBM logic die. Unlike prior PIM/PNM designs that rely on costly internal bandwidth scaling and offload only partial decoding operations, DuoPD enables full decoding execution on PNM by leveraging bandwidth sharing with the GPU over a shared HBM interface. This allows compute-bound prefill and memory -bound decoding to execute concurrently with minimal interference, improving both compute and memory utilization. To realize this design, we develop a compact PNM microarchitecture, a TSV-level bandwidth sharing mechanism, and a hierarchical data mapping scheme tailored for hybrid GPU-PNM execution. Evaluations on server-scale LLMs demonstrate that DuoPD achieves up to 2.23x higher end-to-end throughput than conventional PD-disaggregation.

title: Multi-path Security in Quantum Networks with Trusted Nodes
abstract: Quantum communication networks promise information-theoretic security but this security collapses if intermediate relay nodes are compromised, a risk that grows sharply when compromised nodes cannot be identified. We address this twofold: first, we show that multi-path routing provides quantifiable protection against unidentified compromised nodes. Second, we provide a comprehensive statistical and graph-theoretic analysis of network and node security under compromise, covering full and partial node compromise, optimal placement of additional edges via an iterative method, and comparative hacking-probability analysis across network topologies. Together, these results identify the topology and multi-path routing strategy that most improves security for a given network. We apply this framework to quantum key distribution across multiple network topologies, demonstrating a scalable route to secure, reliable quantum communication under realistic, unidentified adversarial threats, without relying on quantum memory .

title: Superposed analog memory for vector storage in neural networks
abstract: The growing memory demands of artificial neural networks pose a major challenge for energy-efficient computing, particularly for models that rely on large collections of high-dimensional weight and embedding vectors. Conventional memory architectures store these vectors individually, requiring many memory cells per vector and limiting achievable storage density. Here we demonstrate an analog memory architecture that encodes multiple vectors in a distributed superposition within a single memory array. Individual vectors are recovered through in-memory matrix-vector multiplication, allowing the degree of superposition to be tuned to balance storage density against recall fidelity. This approach introduces a new scaling dimension for analog memory, in which effective storage density can be increased without a corresponding increase in the number of physical memory cells. The distributed representation also provides resilience to device-level noise. We implement the architecture on a prototype phase-change memory chip and experimentally evaluate it using embedding tables from deep learning recommendation models and large language models. The results demonstrate inference accuracy comparable to full-precision software baselines, establishing analog superposition as a promising route towards dense, energy-efficient memory for artificial intelligence.

title: Distributing Quantum Circuits Using Pre-Distributed Entanglement Pairs over Quantum Networks
abstract: Distributing quantum circuits across a network of quantum devices is a recent approach to improve the scalability of quantum computation. Entangled pairs of qubits distributed across network nodes are used as a communication resource for executing inter-node (remote) gates. However, establishing these entanglement pairs incurs significant latency, and doing so during the circuit's execution may lead to the decoherence of logical qubits. Instead, it may be beneficial to distribute certain entanglement pairs before the circuit is executed. Thus, we consider the problem of distributing a quantum circuit across a quantum network containing some pre-distributed entanglement pairs and seek to minimize the execution time of the circuit. We address this problem in three steps. First, given the quantum network and (optionally) a probability distribution over training circuits, we determine a set of pre-distributed entanglement pairs under a specified budget. Second, we compute a qubit-to- memory allocation that minimizes the expected execution time given these pre-distributed resources. Finally, we identify any additional entanglement pairs required during execution, generate them concurrently, and execute the circuit gates. We evaluate our methods on a broad range of benchmark circuits.

title: Blame-aware Recomposition for Secure Compilation Proofs of Low-Level Compartment Isolation
abstract: The security guarantees of existing formally verified compilers for compartmentalized programs in unsafe languages like C stop at a rather high level, assuming a built-in protection mechanism and a block-based memory model. Verifying a concrete, low-level enforcement mechanism for compartment isolation is still a major challenge for current proof techniques. In particular, Abate et al.'s proof technique fails because one of their proof steps, recomposition, essentially requires hiding all information about the code of each compartment, which is not practically achievable at a low level. We propose an extension of their proof technique to a low-level setting where compartments can fully observe each other's code. To do so, we introduce an overlay semantics that allows us to characterize these observations as a form of undefined behaviour, and we use a novel variant of recomposition that we call blame-aware recomposition, which essentially allows recomposing executions as needed in the original high-level proof technique, even if the low-level context observes the code, because this context is ultimately going to be discarded. We apply this new proof to a compartment isolation mechanism that uses a programmable tag-based reference monitor.

title: Procedural Memory for Language Agents: A Neurosymbolic Perspective on Explicit Goal Structure
abstract: Large language models remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks requiring procedural reasoning. We argue that a key cause is the absence of explicit procedural memory: accessible, modifiable knowledge of how tasks are accomplished, distinct from semantic and episodic memory. Goal-Oriented Graphs offer such a representation, encoding goals and prerequisite dependencies as inspectable symbolic structure. We examine their construction, the challenges they pose, and principles for integrating them with neural reasoning.

title: GLOBE: Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit via Unit-Sphere Trajectories
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve problem solving, but models often keep generating after the correct answer is already reachable; the extra steps raise serving costs and may replace a correct intermediate result with an incorrect one. We propose GLOBE (Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit), an online, training-free algorithm that terminates the model's CoT process early. GLOBE embeds each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere and reads the shape of the resulting semantic trajectory. GLOBE first applies a trial phase that generates short trial answers in a separate branch, stopping the main stream on an accepted trial after checking confidence against a threshold. If generation continues, a trajectory phase stops the stream once this path repeatedly reverses direction with little net progress. On five benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, tool calling, and agent memory, GLOBE cuts output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time (E2E) by 51.0% across two models, and achieves a five-task average of 80.58%, comparable to Full CoT.

title: Productive State-Space Exploration for Multi-turn RL in LLM Agents
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Model (LLM) agents in multi-turn, long-horizon environments remains challenging due to inefficient action selection and repetitive behavioral patterns. In particular, agents often become trapped in high-confidence yet unproductive behaviors, repeatedly executing invalid actions or entering action loops that hinder task completion. We observe that these frequently violate environment preconditions, revealing a mismatch between the agent's representation of the internal state and the dynamics of the underlying environment. In addition, repetitive high-confidence actions lead to cyclical behaviors that provide little to no progress towards the goal. We argue that addressing these challenges requires more productive task-aligned exploration to improve the agent's understanding of environment dynamics. Motivated by intrinsic curiosity-driven exploration, we propose a conditional state-space exploration framework that balances task completion with intrinsic information-seeking behavior. Specifically, we introduce an intrinsic reward that penalizes actions whose observation duplicates prior state memory. This provides the benefit of reducing redundant behaviors and encouraging state-space coverage without relying on a general information-theoretic measure. Strong experimental results demonstrate that our approach substantially improves policy learning in multi-turn environments, mitigating invalid actions and repetitive loops.

title: Ferroelastic domain wall driven glassy dynamics and photoresponse in a SrTiO$_3$ (111) two-dimensional electron gas
abstract: The (111) orientation of SrTiO$_3$ (STO)-based heterostructures has emerged as a versatile platform for two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs), yet the influence of STO's polar ferroelastic domain-wall (DW) network on charge transport remains largely unexplored. Here we study AlO$_x$/STO (111) interfaces hosting 2DEGs of different carrier densities. In the lower-density 2DEG, low-temperature transport exhibits thermal hysteresis, slow resistance relaxation, cooling-rate dependence, and memory effects, signaling glasslike electron dynamics. The relaxation is strongly non-monotonic in temperature, increasing below $\sim$80 K, peaking near 25 K, and vanishing below $\sim$12 K, tracking the established evolution of the ferroelastic DW state of bulk STO rather than any electronic energy scale, which identifies the DW network as its origin. These signatures are absent in a second, more metallic interface with much higher carrier density, demonstrating that the electron-DW coupling can be tuned. We further show that polar DWs govern the photoresponse: the persistent photoconductivity rises sharply below $\sim$80 K, coinciding with the onset of DW polarity. Together, these results establish polar ferroelastic DWs as a carrier-density-tunable electronic degree of freedom in STO (111)-based 2DEGs, opening routes to manipulate 2DEG properties through topological defects.

title: CondenseVLA: Learnable History Condensation for Efficient Multi-Frame VLA
abstract: Robot manipulation often depends on short-term cues - such as brief contacts, temporary occlusions, and intermediate object states - that are ambiguous in a single frame and can only be resolved by integrating observations over time. However, injecting historical information solely by enlarging the history window is computationally costly and frequently yields limited gains due to substantial redundancy and task-agnostic, inflexible sampling of observations. We propose CondenseVLA, a multi-frame VLA policy with a learnable decoder-side history condensation module for using short-term visual context in action decoding. Given a sequence of cached per-frame features from the VLM backbone, CondenseVLA distills observation history into a fixed set of slot tokens using learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention. Simple auxiliary regularization penalizes overlap among slot attention maps and decorrelates slot embeddings, encouraging complementary attention and reducing slot redundancy. Across the evaluated tasks, CondenseVLA improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8% (+11.1 percentage points), achieves 97.2% on LIBERO, and reaches 52.8% on real-world tasks. It achieves 21.6% success on memory-dependent RMBench tasks. These results support selective condensation of bounded recent visual evidence for action decoding, while harder multi-observation tasks expose the limits of a finite history window.
